_about: Country nerd facts for the 🤓 Nerd facts pop-up on Countries cards. Keyed by country name as in countries.json. Each fact: [label, text], kid-friendly, 160 characters max.
_verify: Written from memory on 2026-11-18, with populations rounded from 2024-25 estimates. Fact-check before launch.

Algeria: About 47 million people live in Algeria.
The Sahara covers more than 80% of Algeria. Its Tassili n'Ajjer plateau has thousands of ancient rock paintings.
Writer Albert Camus was born in Algeria and won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Angola: About 38 million people live in Angola.
The giant sable antelope, with huge curved horns, lives only in Angola and is a national symbol.
Kizomba, a smooth partner dance now loved around the world, comes from Angola.
Benin: About 14 million people live in Benin.
Singer Angélique Kidjo, winner of several Grammy Awards, is from Benin.
Benin is famous for colorful appliqué cloth banners that tell stories with pictures.
Botswana: About 2.5 million people live in Botswana.
The Okavango River never reaches the sea. It spreads out into a giant delta and soaks into the Kalahari Desert.
Botswana's money is called the pula, which means 'rain,' because rain is so precious there.
Burkina Faso: About 23 million people live in Burkina Faso.
The Grand Mosque of Bobo-Dioulasso is made of mud brick, with wooden poles sticking out of its walls.
Gold and cotton are Burkina Faso's biggest exports.
Burundi: About 14 million people live in Burundi.
Lake Tanganyika, on Burundi's border, is the second-deepest lake in the world.
A small stream in Burundi is said to be the farthest-south source of the mighty Nile River.
Cabo Verde: About half a million people live in Cabo Verde.
Morna, a gentle and soulful style of music, is Cabo Verde's national music and a UNESCO treasure.
Pico do Fogo is a volcano, and families grow coffee and fruit inside its huge crater.
Cameroon: About 29 million people live in Cameroon.
Cameroon has more than 250 local languages, plus French and English as official languages.
Mount Cameroon is one of Africa's most active volcanoes, and runners race up it every year.
Central African Republic: About 5.5 million people live in the Central African Republic.
In Dzanga-Sangha park, hundreds of forest elephants gather in one big clearing to drink.
Almost everyone speaks Sango, along with French.
Chad: About 20 million people live in Chad.
Chad's Bodélé Depression is the dustiest place on Earth. Its dust blows across the ocean and feeds the Amazon rainforest!
Zakouma National Park is famous for big herds of elephants and giraffes.
Comoros: About 850,000 people live in the Comoros.
The coelacanth, a fish thought to be gone for millions of years, was found alive near the Comoros.
Mount Karthala, on the main island, has one of the biggest volcano craters in the world.
Republic of the Congo: About 6 million people live in the Republic of the Congo.
Its capital, Brazzaville, sits right across the Congo River from Kinshasa, another country's capital.
Congolese 'sapeurs' are famous for wearing super-stylish, colorful suits.
Democratic Republic of the Congo: About 110 million people live in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The Congo River is the deepest river in the world, more than 700 feet deep in places.
Congolese rumba music is so loved that UNESCO added it to its list of world treasures in 2021.
Ivory Coast (Côte d'Ivoire): About 31 million people live in Ivory Coast.
French is the official language, and Abidjan is one of the biggest French-speaking cities in the world.
Coupé-décalé, a bouncy dance music style, was born among Ivorian DJs.
Djibouti: About 1.1 million people live in Djibouti.
Lac Abbé has tall chimney-like rock towers that puff steam, while flamingos wade between them.
Whale sharks, the biggest fish in the sea, visit Djibouti's coast every winter.
Egypt: About 116 million people live in Egypt.
Koshari, a mix of rice, lentils, pasta and tomato sauce, is Egypt's national dish.
Ancient Egyptians made one of the first 365-day calendars.
Equatorial Guinea: About 1.9 million people live in Equatorial Guinea.
Its capital, Malabo, is on Bioko Island, not on the mainland.
Bioko Island is home to rare monkeys, like the drill, found in very few places.
Eritrea: About 3.5 million people live in Eritrea.
Asmara has a famous old gas station shaped like an airplane, the Fiat Tagliero.
The Dahlak Archipelago has more than 100 islands surrounded by coral reefs.
Eswatini: About 1.2 million people live in Eswatini.
Eswatini is one of the smallest countries in Africa and one of the last kingdoms in the world.
Hlane Royal National Park protects rhinos, lions and elephants.
Ethiopia: About 130 million people live in Ethiopia.
Ethiopia has its own calendar with 13 months, and it's about 7 years behind the one most countries use!
Injera, a spongy flatbread made from teff grain, is used as a plate and a spoon.
Gabon: About 2.5 million people live in Gabon.
The mandrill, the biggest monkey in the world, with a bright red and blue face, lives in Gabon's forests.
Gabon created 13 national parks in 2002, protecting about a tenth of the country.
Gambia: About 2.8 million people live in the Gambia.
The Gambia is called 'the Smiling Coast of Africa.'
More than 500 kinds of birds have been spotted here, so birdwatchers love it.
Ghana: About 34 million people live in Ghana.
Ghana's Adinkra symbols are printed on cloth, and each one stands for a saying or idea.
Kofi Annan, a leader of the United Nations who won the Nobel Peace Prize, was from Ghana.
Guinea: About 14.5 million people live in Guinea.
Guinea is called the 'water tower of West Africa' because the Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers start there.
Les Ballets Africains, Guinea's national dance company, has toured the whole world.
Guinea-Bissau: About 2.2 million people live in Guinea-Bissau.
Gumbe is Guinea-Bissau's lively traditional music.
The Bijagós Archipelago has about 88 islands, and sea turtles nest on its beaches.
Kenya: About 56 million people live in Kenya.
Wangari Maathai started a movement that planted millions of trees, and she won the Nobel Peace Prize.
Swahili words like 'safari' (journey) and 'hakuna matata' (no worries) are spoken in Kenya.
Lesotho: About 2.3 million people live in Lesotho.
People wear colorful Basotho blankets, and the pointy Basotho hat appears on the flag.
Maletsunyane Falls drops more than 600 feet in one big leap.
Liberia: About 5.6 million people live in Liberia.
Liberia's flag looks like the US flag, but with just one star.
Sapo National Park is a huge rainforest home to rare pygmy hippos.
Libya: About 7.4 million people live in Libya.
The old town of Ghadames, the 'pearl of the desert,' has covered streets that stay cool in the heat.
Libya's Sahara has some of the hottest and driest places on Earth.
Madagascar: About 31 million people live in Madagascar.
Six kinds of baobab tree grow only in Madagascar, and some line the famous Avenue of the Baobabs.
The movie Madagascar starred a lion, a zebra, a giraffe and a hippo, animals that don't actually live there!
Malawi: About 21 million people live in Malawi.
Lake Malawi covers about a fifth of the whole country.
The Gule Wamkulu dance, performed in giant masks, is a UNESCO world treasure.
Mali: About 24 million people live in Mali.
Timbuktu was once a famous city of scholars, with hundreds of thousands of old handwritten books.
Singer Salif Keita, called the 'Golden Voice of Africa,' is from Mali.
Mauritania: About 5 million people live in Mauritania.
One of the longest trains in the world, about 1.5 miles long, carries iron ore across the Sahara here.
The desert town of Chinguetti has old family libraries full of handwritten books.
Mauritius: About 1.3 million people live in Mauritius.
The 'Blue Penny' stamp from Mauritius is one of the rarest stamps in the world.
From the air, sand flowing off its coast looks like an underwater waterfall.
Morocco: About 38 million people live in Morocco.
Chefchaouen is a mountain town painted almost entirely blue.
Many famous movies have filmed their desert scenes at the studios in Ouarzazate.
Mozambique: About 34 million people live in Mozambique.
Dugongs, gentle 'sea cows,' graze on seagrass around the Bazaruto islands.
Ilha de Moçambique, a little island town, gave the whole country its name.
Namibia: About 3 million people live in Namibia.
The Namib is thought to be the oldest desert in the world, about 55 million years old.
Namibia has more cheetahs than any other country.
Niger: About 27 million people live in Niger.
Niger is home to West Africa's last wild giraffes, which wander near villages.
Agadez's Grand Mosque has a tall mud-brick tower that's hundreds of years old.
Nigeria: About 230 million people live in Nigeria.
Author Chinua Achebe wrote Things Fall Apart, one of the most-read books from Africa.
Afrobeats stars like Burna Boy and Wizkid come from Nigeria.
Rwanda: About 14 million people live in Rwanda.
On the last Saturday of each month, Rwandans join Umuganda, a community clean-up day.
Plastic bags have been banned since 2008, making Rwanda one of Africa's cleanest countries.
São Tomé and Príncipe: About 230,000 people live in São Tomé and Príncipe.
Pico Cão Grande is a giant needle-shaped rock tower poking out of the rainforest.
It's the second-smallest country in Africa.
Senegal: About 18.5 million people live in Senegal.
Singer Youssou N'Dour is one of Africa's most famous musicians.
The African Renaissance Monument in Dakar is the tallest statue in Africa.
Seychelles: About 130,000 people live in Seychelles, the fewest of any African country.
Its granite islands are some of the oldest ocean islands on Earth.
Aldabra Atoll is home to about 100,000 giant tortoises.
Sierra Leone: About 8.6 million people live in Sierra Leone.
Its capital, Freetown, has one of the biggest natural harbors in the world.
The Tacugama Sanctuary cares for rescued chimpanzees, the national animal.
Somalia: About 19 million people live in Somalia.
Somalia is called the 'Nation of Poets' because poetry is so loved there.
The Laas Geel caves have colorful rock paintings of cows that are thousands of years old.
South Africa: About 64 million people live in South Africa.
The world's first human heart transplant was done in Cape Town in 1967.
Table Mountain in Cape Town is one of the oldest mountains on Earth.
South Sudan: About 12 million people live in South Sudan.
The Sudd is one of the biggest wetlands in the world.
Cattle are very important in South Sudan and appear in many songs and celebrations.
Sudan: About 50 million people live in Sudan.
The pyramids of Meroë have steep, pointy sides, different from Egypt's.
Ful medames, a hearty bean stew, is a favorite breakfast.
Tanzania: About 68 million people live in Tanzania.
Lake Tanganyika is the longest freshwater lake in the world.
Freddie Mercury, the singer of the band Queen, was born on Zanzibar.
Togo: About 9.5 million people live in Togo.
Togo is very thin: only about 30 miles wide along its coast.
Togo is known for colorful wax-print fabrics sold in Lomé's huge market.
Tunisia: About 12 million people live in Tunisia.
Sidi Bou Said is a cliffside village painted white and bright blue.
Harissa, a spicy red chili paste, is a Tunisian favorite.
Uganda: About 50 million people live in Uganda.
The Rwenzori, the 'Mountains of the Moon,' have snow and glaciers near the equator.
Queen Elizabeth National Park has lions that climb trees and nap in the branches.
Zambia: About 21 million people live in Zambia.
Every year about 10 million fruit bats fly into Kasanka park, one of the biggest animal migrations on Earth.
Lake Kariba, shared with Zimbabwe, is one of the biggest human-made lakes in the world.
Zimbabwe: About 17 million people live in Zimbabwe.
Hwange National Park has one of Africa's biggest elephant herds.
Stone sculptures by Shona artists are famous around the world.
Afghanistan: About 42 million people live in Afghanistan.
Kabuli pulao, rice cooked with carrots and raisins, is the national dish.
The Wakhan Corridor is a long, skinny strip of land that reaches all the way to China.
Armenia: About 3 million people live in Armenia.
Armenia has its own alphabet, created in the year 405 by a scholar named Mesrop Mashtots.
Armenia was the first country to make chess a school subject for kids.
Azerbaijan: About 10 million people live in Azerbaijan.
Azerbaijan has about half of all the mud volcanoes on Earth.
Mugham, Azerbaijan's traditional music, is a UNESCO world treasure.
Bahrain: About 1.6 million people live in Bahrain.
Bahrain hosts a Formula 1 race under bright floodlights in the desert.
Bahrain is a group of islands linked to Saudi Arabia by a 15-mile bridge and causeway.
Bangladesh: About 175 million people live in Bangladesh.
Cox's Bazar has one of the longest natural beaches in the world, about 75 miles long.
Muhammad Yunus won the Nobel Peace Prize for tiny loans that help people start small businesses.
Bhutan: Bhutan's forests soak up more carbon than the country makes.
Brunei: The Sultan's palace is one of the biggest homes in the world, with about 1,800 rooms.
About 70% of Brunei is covered in rainforest.
Cambodia: About 17.5 million people live in Cambodia.
Fish amok, fish steamed in banana leaves with coconut curry, is a national dish.
Tonlé Sap lake grows about five times bigger in the rainy season.
China: About 1.4 billion people live in China.
Wild giant pandas live only in the mountains of China.
More people speak Mandarin Chinese as their first language than any other language.
Georgia: About 3.7 million people live in Georgia.
Georgia has its own alphabet, with 33 curly letters.
Georgian polyphonic singing, with many voices weaving together, is a UNESCO treasure.
India: India has the most people of any country: about 1.45 billion.
India makes more movies every year than any other country. Bollywood is in Mumbai.
Yoga began in India thousands of years ago.
Indonesia: About 280 million people live in Indonesia.
Indonesia has more active volcanoes than any other country.
Batik, cloth decorated with wax and dye patterns, is a famous Indonesian art.
Iran: About 90 million people live in Iran.
Nowruz, the Persian New Year, starts on the first day of spring.
Isfahan's Naqsh-e Jahan Square is one of the biggest city squares in the world.
Iraq: About 46 million people live in Iraq.
Ancient Mesopotamians counted in 60s, which is why an hour has 60 minutes.
Babylon, one of the most famous cities of the ancient world, was in Iraq.
Israel: About 10 million people live in Israel.
The USB flash drive and the Waze navigation app were invented in Israel.
Falafel and hummus are everyday favorites.
Japan: About 124 million people live in Japan.
Japan is made up of about 14,000 islands.
Instant noodles were invented in Japan in 1958.
Jordan: About 11.5 million people live in Jordan.
Jordan's red desert valleys played the planet Mars in the movie The Martian.
The Dead Sea, on Jordan's border, is the lowest place on land on Earth.
Kazakhstan: About 20 million people live in Kazakhstan.
Charyn Canyon is nicknamed the little brother of the Grand Canyon.
The capital, Astana, has a tower shaped like a tree holding a golden egg.
Kuwait: About 4.9 million people live in Kuwait.
The Kuwaiti dinar is one of the most valuable currencies in the world.
Kuwait has no rivers at all.
Kyrgyzstan: About 7 million people live in Kyrgyzstan.
Issyk-Kul is one of the biggest mountain lakes in the world, and it never freezes.
The Epic of Manas is one of the longest poems ever told, with about half a million lines.
Laos: About 7.7 million people live in Laos.
Laos is the only Southeast Asian country with no coastline.
The Plain of Jars is covered with thousands of giant stone jars from long ago.
Lebanon: About 5.8 million people live in Lebanon.
Lebanon's name comes from an old word for 'white,' after its snowy mountains.
Byblos is one of the oldest cities on Earth, and the word 'Bible' comes from its name.
Malaysia: About 35 million people live in Malaysia.
The rafflesia, the biggest flower in the world, blooms in Malaysia's rainforests.
Orangutans, whose name means 'person of the forest,' live in Malaysian Borneo.
Maldives: About half a million people live in the Maldives.
Some Maldives beaches glow blue at night, lit up by tiny sea plankton.
The Maldives is famous for hotel rooms built on stilts over the water.
Mongolia: About 3.5 million people live in Mongolia.
The first dinosaur eggs ever recognized by scientists were found in Mongolia's Gobi Desert in the 1920s.
The Naadam festival features wrestling, horse racing and archery.
Myanmar: About 54 million people live in Myanmar.
Fishermen on Inle Lake row their boats with one leg.
Many people wear thanaka, a yellow paste made from tree bark, on their faces as sunscreen.
Nepal: About 30 million people live in Nepal.
Nepal is the only country whose flag isn't a rectangle. It's two stacked triangles!
Chitwan National Park is home to one-horned rhinos and Bengal tigers.
North Korea: About 26 million people live in North Korea.
Mount Kumgang, the 'Diamond Mountain,' is famous for its jagged rocky peaks.
Kimchi, spicy fermented cabbage, is eaten with almost every meal.
Oman: About 5 million people live in Oman.
Wadi Shab has turquoise pools you can swim through to a waterfall hidden in a cave.
Green sea turtles come ashore to nest on Ras al Jinz beach.
Pakistan: About 250 million people live in Pakistan.
Three huge mountain ranges meet in Pakistan: the Himalayas, the Karakoram and the Hindu Kush.
Malala Yousafzai became the youngest Nobel Peace Prize winner ever, at age 17.
Palestine: About 5.5 million people live in Palestine.
Jericho is one of the oldest cities in the world, and Bethlehem is a famous old town.
Musakhan, roasted chicken on flatbread with onions and sumac, is a national dish.
Philippines: About 115 million people live in the Philippines.
The Chocolate Hills are more than 1,200 round hills that turn brown in the dry season.
The tarsier, a tiny primate with giant eyes, lives in the Philippines.
Qatar: About 3 million people live in Qatar.
At Khor Al Adaid, the 'Inland Sea,' giant sand dunes run right into the sea.
Doha's Museum of Islamic Art sits on its own little island.
Saudi Arabia: About 35 million people live in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia is the biggest country in the world with no permanent rivers.
Kabsa, spiced rice with chicken or lamb, is the national dish.
Singapore: About 6 million people live in Singapore.
Selling chewing gum is banned in Singapore to help keep the streets clean.
Singapore's airport has the Jewel, a giant indoor waterfall surrounded by a forest.
South Korea: About 51 million people live in South Korea.
Taekwondo, a martial art with high kicks, comes from Korea.
South Korea has some of the fastest internet in the world.
Sri Lanka: About 22 million people live in Sri Lanka.
Sigiriya, the 'Lion Rock,' has the ruins of a palace on top of a giant rock.
Sri Lanka had the world's first woman prime minister, Sirimavo Bandaranaike, in 1960.
Syria: About 24 million people live in Syria.
One of the world's first alphabets was written in Ugarit, an ancient city in Syria.
Kibbeh and fattoush salad are favorite Syrian foods.
Taiwan: About 23 million people live in Taiwan.
The Formosan black bear, with a white V on its chest, is a national symbol.
At the Pingxi Lantern Festival, thousands of glowing sky lanterns float into the night.
Tajikistan: About 10.5 million people live in Tajikistan.
Ismoil Somoni Peak, its tallest mountain, is more than 24,000 feet high.
Tajik is a close cousin of the Persian language.
Thailand: About 72 million people live in Thailand.
Bangkok's full name in Thai is one of the longest city names in the world.
Songkran, the Thai New Year, is celebrated with giant water fights in the streets.
Timor-Leste: About 1.4 million people live in Timor-Leste.
Timor-Leste has two official languages: Tetum and Portuguese.
Tais, colorful hand-woven cloth, is a UNESCO world treasure.
Türkiye (Turkey): About 86 million people live in Türkiye.
Istanbul is a giant city that sits on two continents: Europe and Asia.
In Cappadocia, hot air balloons float over rock towers nicknamed 'fairy chimneys.'
Turkmenistan: About 7 million people live in Turkmenistan.
The Karakum Desert covers about 80% of the country.
Turkmen carpets are so important that carpet patterns appear on the flag.
United Arab Emirates: About 11 million people live in the United Arab Emirates.
In 2021 the UAE's Hope probe reached Mars, the first Arab mission to another planet.
Abu Dhabi's Sheikh Zayed Mosque has one of the biggest hand-knotted carpets in the world.
Uzbekistan: About 37 million people live in Uzbekistan.
Uzbekistan is one of only two countries surrounded by countries that also have no coast.
Round non bread is stamped with pretty patterns before it's baked in clay ovens.
Vietnam: About 101 million people live in Vietnam.
Son Doong is the biggest cave in the world, with its own jungle and clouds inside.
Water puppetry, with puppets dancing across a pond, is a Vietnamese art.
Yemen: About 40 million people live in Yemen.
Socotra Island has umbrella-shaped trees and plants found nowhere else on Earth.
Sanaa's old houses are decorated with white patterns that look like gingerbread icing.
Albania: About 2.7 million people live in Albania.
The Blue Eye is a bright blue spring so clear you can see deep down into the water.
Traditionally, many Albanians nod to say 'no' and shake their heads to say 'yes.'
Andorra: Andorra has two princes at once: the President of France and a bishop from Spain.
Austria: About 9.2 million people live in Austria.
The snow globe was invented in Vienna around 1900.
The Vienna Boys' Choir has been singing for more than 500 years.
Belarus: About 9.2 million people live in Belarus.
Belarus has more than 10,000 lakes, so it's nicknamed the 'Land of Blue Lakes.'
Painter Marc Chagall, famous for his dreamy, colorful art, was born in Belarus.
Belgium: About 11.8 million people live in Belgium.
The saxophone was invented by a Belgian named Adolphe Sax.
Belgium has three official languages: Dutch, French and German.
Bosnia and Herzegovina: About 3.2 million people live in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Burek, a flaky spiral pastry filled with meat or cheese, is a favorite.
The Una River is famous for its emerald-green water and waterfalls.
Bulgaria: About 6.4 million people live in Bulgaria.
The Cyrillic alphabet, used by millions of people today, was developed in Bulgaria long ago.
Each March, Bulgarians wear red-and-white martenitsa bracelets to welcome spring.
Croatia: About 3.9 million people live in Croatia.
The spotted Dalmatian dog is named after Croatia's Dalmatia region.
Dubrovnik's old town was a filming spot for Star Wars: The Last Jedi.
Cyprus: About 1.3 million people live in Cyprus.
Cyprus is one of the sunniest places in Europe.
Loggerhead and green sea turtles nest on its beaches every summer.
Czechia (Czech Republic): About 10.9 million people live in Czechia.
Prague's astronomical clock, built in 1410, still ticks today.
The word 'robot' was first used in a Czech play in 1920.
Denmark: About 6 million people live in Denmark.
Copenhagen has more bikes than cars.
Hygge, a Danish word for a cozy, happy feeling, is now used around the world.
Estonia: About 1.4 million people live in Estonia.
Estonia's Song Festival brings together about 30,000 singers on one stage.
About half of Estonia is covered in forest.
Finland: About 5.6 million people live in Finland.
The Moomins were created by Finnish author and artist Tove Jansson.
Finland hosts funny world championships, like air guitar and mobile phone throwing.
France: About 68 million people live in France.
France is the most visited country in the world.
Louis Braille invented the Braille reading system for blind people when he was a teenager.
Germany: About 84 million people live in Germany.
Composer Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn, Germany.
Greece: About 10.4 million people live in Greece.
Greece has about 6,000 islands, and only around 200 have people living on them.
The marathon race is named after Marathon, a town in Greece.
Hungary: About 9.6 million people live in Hungary.
Budapest sits on more than 100 hot springs, and people swim in warm outdoor baths in winter.
The ballpoint pen was invented by Hungarian journalist László Bíró.
Iceland: Iceland has no mosquitoes at all.
Iceland heats most of its homes with hot water from deep underground.
Ireland: About 5.3 million people live in Ireland.
The harp is Ireland's national symbol, and it's even on Irish coins.
Authors James Joyce and Oscar Wilde were both from Ireland.
Italy: About 59 million people live in Italy.
Alessandro Volta invented the electric battery, and the word 'volt' is named after him.
Venice is built on about 118 small islands linked by around 400 bridges.
Kosovo: About 1.6 million people live in Kosovo.
Kosovo has one of the youngest populations in Europe.
The Mirusha waterfalls are a chain of lakes and falls in a rocky canyon.
Latvia: About 1.9 million people live in Latvia.
Riga has one of the biggest collections of Art Nouveau buildings in the world.
Latvians say the first decorated Christmas tree stood in Riga in 1510.
Liechtenstein: Liechtenstein is surrounded by countries that also have no coast, one of only two in the world.
All of Liechtenstein's Olympic medals have been won in skiing.
Lithuania: About 2.9 million people live in Lithuania.
Lithuanian is one of the oldest languages still spoken in Europe.
Basketball is Lithuania's most loved sport.
Luxembourg: In 2020 Luxembourg made buses, trams and trains free for everyone.
People speak Luxembourgish, French and German.
North Macedonia: About 1.8 million people live in North Macedonia.
Mother Teresa, famous for helping people in need, was born in Skopje.
Skopje's Old Bazaar is one of the biggest old markets in the Balkans.
Malta: Maltese is related to Arabic but is written with the same letters as English.
Malta's Popeye Village was built as a movie set for the 1980 Popeye movie.
Moldova: About 2.4 million people live in Moldova.
Moldova has rich black soil that is some of the best farmland in Europe.
At Orheiul Vechi, a little monastery is carved right into a cliff.
Monaco: Part of Monaco was built on land made by filling in the sea.
Ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau ran Monaco's Oceanographic Museum.
Montenegro: The Tara River Canyon is the deepest canyon in Europe.
Sveti Stefan is a tiny island village joined to the beach by a thin sandy path.
Netherlands: About 18 million people live in the Netherlands.
There are more bikes than people in the Netherlands.
Dutch lens makers built some of the first microscopes and telescopes.
Norway: About 5.6 million people live in Norway.
Every year, Norway gives London a giant Christmas tree as a thank-you gift.
In summer, the sun never sets in northern Norway. It's called the midnight sun.
Poland: About 37 million people live in Poland.
Marie Curie, the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, was born in Warsaw.
The Wieliczka Salt Mine has chapels and statues carved entirely out of salt.
Portugal: About 10.6 million people live in Portugal.
Portuguese is spoken by about 250 million people around the world.
Lisbon's old yellow trams rattle up and down its steep hills.
Romania: About 19 million people live in Romania.
The Danube Delta is one of the best places in Europe to see pelicans and other birds.
Romania's Palace of the Parliament is one of the heaviest buildings in the world.
Russia: About 144 million people live in Russia.
Lake Baikal holds about a fifth of all the fresh water in the world's lakes and rivers.
Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev created the periodic table of the elements.
San Marino: About 34,000 people live in San Marino.
San Marino is completely surrounded by Italy.
The three towers on Mount Titano appear on San Marino's flag.
Serbia: About 6.6 million people live in Serbia.
Inventor Nikola Tesla, who helped bring electricity into homes, was born to Serbian parents.
Ajvar, a sweet red pepper spread, is a Serbian favorite.
Slovakia: About 5.4 million people live in Slovakia.
Slovakia makes more cars per person than any other country.
Dobšiná Ice Cave stays frozen all year, even in summer.
Slovenia: About 2.1 million people live in Slovenia.
Postojna Cave is home to the olm, a pale cave salamander nicknamed the 'baby dragon.'
Slovenia loves bees so much that it suggested World Bee Day to the United Nations.
Spain: About 49 million people live in Spain.
At La Tomatina, a festival in Buñol, thousands of people throw tomatoes at each other.
Miguel de Cervantes wrote Don Quixote, one of the most famous novels ever.
Sweden: About 10.6 million people live in Sweden.
Sweden's Icehotel is rebuilt out of ice and snow every winter.
Swedish engineer Nils Bohlin invented the modern three-point seat belt in 1959.
Switzerland: About 9 million people live in Switzerland.
Switzerland has four official languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh.
The World Wide Web was born at CERN, a science lab near Geneva.
Ukraine: Ukraine is the biggest country entirely inside Europe.
Pysanky are eggs decorated with beautiful wax-and-dye patterns.
Varenyky, dumplings filled with potato, cheese or cherries, are a favorite.
United Kingdom: About 69 million people live in the United Kingdom.
Scottish inventor John Logie Baird showed the first working television in 1926.
J.K. Rowling wrote the Harry Potter books in the UK.
Vatican City: Only about 800 people live in Vatican City.
The Vatican has its own post office, radio station and tiny railway station.
Michelangelo spent four years painting the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.
Antigua and Barbuda: About 94,000 people live in Antigua and Barbuda.
Antigua Sailing Week is one of the biggest sailboat races in the Caribbean.
Barbuda has one of the biggest frigatebird colonies in the world.
Bahamas: About 410,000 people live in the Bahamas.
Dean's Blue Hole is one of the deepest underwater sinkholes in the world.
Junkanoo is a colorful street parade with drums, whistles and cowbells.
Barbados: Cricket legend Sir Garfield Sobers is from Barbados.
Crop Over is a big summer festival that began as a party for the end of the sugarcane harvest.
Belize: Cockscomb Basin is the world's first wildlife reserve made for jaguars.
English is Belize's official language, the only Central American country where it is.
Canada: About 41 million people live in Canada.
Insulin, a medicine that helps millions of people with diabetes, was discovered in Canada in 1921.
Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined.
Costa Rica: About 5.2 million people live in Costa Rica.
'Pura vida,' meaning 'pure life,' is used to say hello, goodbye and everything's great.
Costa Rica has had no army since 1948 and spends that money on schools and parks.
Cuba: About 10 million people live in Cuba.
The bee hummingbird, the smallest bird in the world, lives only in Cuba.
Mambo and cha-cha-chá music and dancing started in Cuba.
Dominica: Dominica's flag shows the Sisserou parrot, a bird found only on the island.
Parts of the Pirates of the Caribbean movies were filmed in Dominica.
Dominican Republic: About 11.4 million people live in the Dominican Republic.
Santo Domingo is the oldest city founded by Europeans in the Americas.
Pico Duarte is the tallest mountain in the Caribbean.
El Salvador: About 6.3 million people live in El Salvador.
It's the only Central American country without a Caribbean coastline.
Its Pacific beaches are famous with surfers from around the world.
Grenada: Grenada's Underwater Sculpture Park has dozens of statues on the sea floor.
Oil down, a one-pot stew with breadfruit and coconut milk, is the national dish.
Guatemala: About 18 million people live in Guatemala.
Guatemala has more than 30 volcanoes, and some puff smoke almost every day.
The colorful quetzal bird is the national bird, and Guatemala's money is named after it.
Haiti: About 11.8 million people live in Haiti.
Soup joumou, a hearty pumpkin soup, is eaten on New Year's Day to celebrate freedom.
Haitian painters and metal artists are famous for their bright, joyful art.
Honduras: About 10.8 million people live in Honduras.
The island of Roatán sits on the second-biggest barrier reef in the world.
The music and dance of the Garifuna people are a UNESCO world treasure.
Jamaica: About 2.8 million people live in Jamaica.
Jamaica's name comes from a Taíno word meaning 'land of wood and water.'
Jamaica's bobsled team inspired the movie Cool Runnings.
Mexico: About 131 million people live in Mexico.
Mexico City was built on top of an old lake, and parts of it slowly sink every year.
More people speak Spanish in Mexico than in any other country.
Nicaragua: About 7 million people live in Nicaragua.
Visitors can sandboard down Cerro Negro, one of the youngest volcanoes in Central America.
Poet Rubén Darío is a national hero and one of the most famous poets in Spanish.
Panama: About 4.5 million people live in Panama.
On a clear day, you can see both the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans from Panama's tallest volcano.
Panama has more kinds of birds than the United States and Canada combined.
Saint Kitts and Nevis: About 47,000 people live in Saint Kitts and Nevis.
Mount Liamuiga is a sleeping volcano with a lake inside its crater.
Green vervet monkeys roam the islands in big, playful troops.
Saint Lucia: About 180,000 people live in Saint Lucia.
Saint Lucia has two Nobel Prize winners, the most per person of any country.
The Saint Lucia Jazz Festival draws music lovers from around the world.
Saint Vincent and the Grenadines: About 100,000 people live in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.
Wallilabou Bay was a filming spot for the Pirates of the Caribbean movies.
La Soufrière, a volcano at the north end of Saint Vincent, has a lake in its crater.
Trinidad and Tobago: About 1.5 million people live in Trinidad and Tobago.
At sunset in the Caroni Swamp, flocks of bright red scarlet ibises fly home to roost.
Pitch Lake is the biggest natural lake of asphalt in the world.
United States: About 340 million people live in the United States.
Yellowstone, created in 1872, was the first national park in the world.
Inventor Thomas Edison got more than 1,000 patents, including one for the phonograph.
Argentina: About 46 million people live in Argentina.
Aconcagua is the tallest mountain in the world outside of Asia.
Iguazú Falls, on the border with Brazil, is made up of about 275 waterfalls.
Bolivia: About 12.5 million people live in Bolivia.
La Paz and El Alto have the highest and longest city cable car network in the world.
Bolivia has two capitals: Sucre and La Paz.
Brazil: About 213 million people live in Brazil.
Brazil has more kinds of plants and animals than any other country.
Rio de Janeiro's Carnival is one of the biggest parties on Earth.
Chile: About 20 million people live in Chile.
The Atacama Desert is so dry and clear that astronomers build giant telescopes there.
Chilean poets Gabriela Mistral and Pablo Neruda both won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
Colombia: About 53 million people live in Colombia.
Caño Cristales is called the 'river of five colors' because of bright red plants in its water.
Author Gabriel García Márquez, who won the Nobel Prize, was from Colombia.
Ecuador: About 18 million people live in Ecuador.
Ecuador is Spanish for 'equator,' the line that runs right through the country.
The top of Chimborazo volcano is the farthest point on Earth from the planet's center.
Guyana: The giant Victoria water lily, with pads big enough to hold a small child, is the national flower.
Giant river otters and jaguars live in Guyana's rainforests.
Paraguay: About 7 million people live in Paraguay.
Most Paraguayans speak both Spanish and Guaraní, a native language.
The Itaipú Dam, shared with Brazil, is one of the biggest power plants in the world.
Peru: About 34 million people live in Peru.
Lake Titicaca, shared with Bolivia, is the highest lake in the world that big boats sail on.
Ceviche, fresh fish soaked in lime juice, is Peru's national dish.
Suriname: In the capital, Paramaribo, a mosque and a synagogue stand side by side as friendly neighbors.
Giant leatherback sea turtles nest on Suriname's beaches.
Uruguay: About 3.4 million people live in Uruguay.
Uruguay was the first country to give a laptop to every public school kid.
Uruguay makes almost all of its electricity from wind, water and sun.
Venezuela: About 28 million people live in Venezuela.
Lightning flashes over Lake Maracaibo on about 140 to 160 nights a year, more than almost anywhere.
Paradise Falls in the movie Up was inspired by Venezuela's flat-topped tepui mountains.
Australia: About 27 million people live in Australia.
The Great Barrier Reef is the biggest living structure on Earth.
Fiji: 'Bula!' is the cheerful Fijian way to say hello.
The 180-degree line, halfway around the world, runs right across Fiji's Taveuni island.
Kiribati: Kiritimati, or Christmas Island, is the biggest coral atoll on Earth by land.
Marshall Islands: About 42,000 people live in the Marshall Islands.
The capital, Majuro, is a thin ring of land around a lagoon.
Its waters are one of the biggest shark sanctuaries in the world.
Micronesia: Micronesia has 607 islands spread across a huge area of the Pacific Ocean.
The island of Pohnpei is one of the rainiest places on Earth.
Nauru: Nauru is the third-smallest country in the world.
Nauru has no official capital city.
New Zealand: About 5.3 million people live in New Zealand.
In 1893 New Zealand became the first country where women could vote in national elections.
New Zealand has about five sheep for every person.
Palau: Palau's Rock Islands are hundreds of mushroom-shaped green islands.
Visitors sign the Palau Pledge, a promise in their passport to protect nature.
Papua New Guinea: More than 10 million people live in Papua New Guinea.
The world's biggest butterfly, Queen Alexandra's birdwing, lives only here.
The Goroka Show brings together groups in colorful feathers and face paint.
Samoa: Traditional Samoan houses, called fale, have no walls, just a roof on posts.
Palusami, taro leaves baked in coconut cream, is a favorite dish.
Solomon Islands: About 750,000 people live in the Solomon Islands.
Marovo Lagoon is one of the biggest saltwater lagoons in the world.
Lake Tegano on Rennell Island is the biggest lake in the Pacific Islands.
Tonga: Tonga is the only kingdom among the Pacific Islands, with a king and royal family.
Tonga is one of the first countries to start each new day.
Tuvalu: Tuvalu's highest point is only about 15 feet above sea level.
Funafuti's airport runway doubles as a soccer field and hangout spot when no planes are coming.
Vanuatu: Land diving on Pentecost Island, jumping from tall towers with vines tied to the ankles, inspired bungee jumping.
Vanuatu has more than 100 languages, one of the most per person of any country.
